etymology: From Latin trans (across) and substantia (substance), coined to name a supposed change of underlying being; defined dogmatically at the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and Trent (1551).
biblical_def: Transubstantiation is the Roman dogma that, at the priest's consecration, the whole substance of the bread is changed into the substance of Christ's body and the whole substance of the wine into His blood, the outward appearances alone remaining. Scripture will not bear this weight. When our Lord said “This is my body,” He spoke as He often did in figure—“I am the door,” “I am the vine”—and He stood bodily before the disciples, holding bread in His hand, plainly distinct from it. The dogma collides head-on with the finished work of Calvary, for the priest claims to offer Christ afresh as a propitiatory sacrifice, whereas Hebrews testifies that by one offering He hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified. A sacrifice repeated is a sacrifice unfinished; but our great High Priest sat down, His work complete. The Reformed faith confesses instead a true spiritual presence: in the Supper the believer, by faith and through the Holy Spirit, feeds really upon the crucified and risen Christ, not by any carnal grinding with the teeth but by the soul's laying hold of Him. The elements remain bread and wine, signs and seals of the covenant. To bow before the consecrated host is therefore idolatry, worshipping a creature in place of the Creator. We hold fast the apostolic ordinance: do this in remembrance of Me.
webster_summary: The Roman doctrine that the bread and wine of the Mass are converted in substance into the actual body and blood of Christ.
webster_full: TRANSUBSTANTIATION, noun [Latin trans, across, and substantia, substance.] In the Roman church, the supposed conversion of the whole substance of the bread and wine in the eucharist into the body and blood of Christ, the accidents alone remaining.
A doctrine defined at the Lateran Council of 1215 and anathematized against by the Reformed churches.
Distinguished from the Lutheran consubstantiation and from the Reformed confession of a spiritual presence received by faith.
The ground of the Roman Mass, condemned as a renewed offering of Christ contrary to Scripture.
“For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.” Hebrews 10:14.
scriptures: For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.
And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me.
But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God;
corruption_summary: Rome corrupts the Supper by teaching that the substance of bread and wine literally becomes Christ's flesh and blood, making the Mass a repeated propitiatory sacrifice and the host an object of worship.
corruption_paragraphs: The Roman doctrine of transubstantiation, fixed at Lateran IV and Trent, holds that after consecration nothing of bread and wine remains but their accidents, the substance having been changed into Christ's very body and blood. From this follows the adoration of the host and the sacrifice of the Mass. Scripture refutes both. Hebrews insists that Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for ever and then sat down; a finished work cannot be repeated upon ten thousand altars. To re-present Him as a sin-offering is to deny that “It is finished” meant what it said.

Against the carnal eating Rome demands, the Reformed faith confesses that believers feed upon Christ truly but spiritually, by faith and through the Spirit, while the elements remain bread and wine—signs and seals, not the thing signified. To bend the knee before a wafer is idolatry, ascribing to a creature the worship due God alone. We recover the plain words of institution: “this do in remembrance of me,” a memorial and communion, not a sacrifice and not a transmutation.
roots_summary: The root joins Latin trans, across, to substantia, the underlying being of a thing.
roots_lines: trans — Latin, across, over, beyond.
substantia — Latin, that which stands under; underlying essence.
Combined to assert a change of essence beneath unchanged appearances.
A scholastic category imported to defend the Mass, not drawn from Scripture.
The Reformed answer keeps substance and sign distinct, joined only sacramentally.
usage: The Reformer preached against transubstantiation, showing from Hebrews that one offering had perfected the saints for ever.
Because transubstantiation makes the Mass a renewed sacrifice, it overthrows the sufficiency of the cross.
Where Rome adores the host, the Reformed believer lifts his heart to the Christ enthroned above, feeding on Him by faith.

etymology: From the name of Martin Luther (1483–1546), with the suffix -ism denoting a body of doctrine; the tradition flowing from his recovery of the gospel.
biblical_def: Lutheranism is the confessional tradition that descends from Martin Luther's recovery of the gospel in the sixteenth century. We owe Luther a debt that cannot be overstated, for under God he thundered against the indulgence-trade and lifted up justification by faith alone, apart from the works of the law. His cry of sola fide and sola scriptura opened the door to all that followed, and the Reformed churches gladly own him as a father in the faith. Yet on certain points Lutheranism halted where Scripture would have carried it further. It teaches a sacramental union in the Supper—that Christ's body and blood are received in, with, and under the bread and wine—and to uphold this it asserts the ubiquity of Christ's glorified body, that His humanity is everywhere present. The Reformed faith answers that the man Christ Jesus is locally in heaven according to His human nature, while believers feed on Him spiritually by the Spirit who unites things distant. Further, the Lutheran scheme draws back from definite atonement, holding that Christ died for all without exception, which loosens the golden chain of redemption. We honor the tradition's witness to grace while we press on to the fuller confession of God's sovereign and particular saving purpose set down in our standards.
webster_summary: The body of doctrine and the churches deriving from Martin Luther, holding justification by faith yet differing from the Reformed on the Supper and the extent of the atonement.
webster_full: LUTHERANISM, noun [from Martin Luther.] The doctrines and ecclesiastical system of the churches that follow the teaching of Luther, summarized in the Augsburg Confession.
Distinguished chiefly by its zeal for justification by faith alone and the supreme authority of Scripture.
Holds a sacramental union in the Lord's Supper, the body of Christ present in, with, and under the elements.
Departs from the Reformed in teaching the ubiquity of Christ's body and a universal atonement.
“The just shall live by faith.” Romans 1:17, the text that loosed Luther's chains.
scriptures: Rom 1:17
For therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith: as it is written, The just shall live by faith.
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
Act 1:11
Which also said, Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven.
corruption_summary: This entry concerns a Protestant tradition we honor in part; its errors are confessional, not a postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the consistency of grace. Lutheranism rightly recovered justification by faith alone, yet stopped short of the doctrine's full harvest: if salvation is by grace alone and faith itself is God's gift, then the atonement that purchased it must be definite, securing all for whom it was offered. To hold that Christ died alike for those who perish is to leave His blood, in some, spilt in vain.

Likewise the sacramental union and the ubiquity of Christ's body strain the bounds of His true humanity. Scripture confesses that this same Jesus was taken up into heaven and shall so come again—His body is real, local, and glorified above, not diffused through the elements of every altar. The Reformed confession honors Luther's courage while completing his reform, feeding the soul on Christ by the Spirit and resting wholly in a particular, effectual redemption.
roots_summary: The word is simply the surname of the German Reformer fashioned into a name for his movement.
roots_lines: Luther — the family name of Martin Luther of Saxony.
-an — suffix marking one belonging to or following.
-ism — suffix denoting a system of doctrine.
First applied by opponents, later worn by the churches themselves.
Names a tradition kin to, yet distinct from, the Reformed.
usage: Lutheranism preserved the gospel of free grace when Rome had buried it under merit and indulgence.
On the Supper, Lutheranism and the Reformed parted, the one teaching a bodily presence, the other a spiritual feeding by faith.
We thank God for Lutheranism's witness to sola fide even as we confess a particular atonement it would not embrace.

etymology: Named for the city of its publication, London, and the Baptist churches that owned it; the “second” distinguishing it from the First London Confession of 1644.
biblical_def: The Second London Baptist Confession is the primary subordinate standard of this dictionary and the fullest creedal expression of the Reformed Baptist faith. Drawn up in 1677 during years of persecution and published openly in 1689 once liberty came, it was subscribed by the messengers of more than a hundred congregations. The framers deliberately followed the language of the Westminster Confession and the Congregationalists' Savoy Declaration, that the world might see how nearly the Baptists stood with their paedobaptist brethren in the great doctrines of grace—the sovereignty of God, the covenant of grace, total depravity, unconditional election, particular redemption, effectual calling, justification by faith alone, and the perseverance of the saints. Where they differed they spoke plainly. Baptism, they confessed, belongs only to those who actually profess repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, and it is rightly administered by immersion. The church is a gathered company of visible saints, not a parish of all comers. And the civil magistrate, while owed honor and obedience in lawful things, has no authority to compel conscience in worship. So the Confession joins the broad stream of Reformed orthodoxy while pressing the regulative principle of worship and the believer's baptism to their consistent end. It remains our chief witness, under Scripture, of what we believe and why.
webster_summary: The 1689 confession of the Particular Baptists, modeled on Westminster, and the principal subordinate standard of Reformed Baptist churches.
webster_full: SECOND LONDON BAPTIST CONFESSION, noun [from London, place of issue, and Baptist.] The confession of faith composed by the Particular Baptists in 1677 and publicly subscribed in 1689.
Built upon the framework of the Westminster Confession and the Savoy Declaration.
Confesses the doctrines of sovereign grace held in common with Reformed paedobaptists.
Departs in its articles on baptism, the gathered church, and the limits of the magistrate.
“Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught.” Titus 1:9.
scriptures: Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Act 2:41
Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: A confessional standard, not the object of any postmodern redefinition; the danger is neglect rather than corruption.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is confessional integrity. In an age that prizes the bare “no creed but the Bible,” many churches drift doctrinally for want of a tested standard. The 1689 does not stand over Scripture but under it, gathering the church's settled understanding so that error may be named and the faith once delivered may be guarded and handed on.

The Confession also rebukes the modern temptation to make worship a matter of taste and the church a voluntary club of all comers. By the regulative principle it confesses that God alone prescribes how He will be worshipped, and by believer's baptism it confesses a church of professing saints. To recover the 1689 is to recover careful doctrine, ordered worship, and a regenerate membership—Jude's charge to contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints.
roots_summary: The title is descriptive: the second confession issued by Baptists at London.
roots_lines: second — following the First London Confession of 1644.
London — the city where it was drafted and published.
Baptist — from Greek baptizo, to immerse; the churches confessing believer's baptism.
confession — Latin confiteor, to acknowledge openly.
Composed 1677, subscribed and printed openly in 1689.
usage: The elders examined the candidate against the Second London Baptist Confession before ordaining him.
Chapter 26 of the 1689 sets forth the gathered church of visible saints, not a mixed parish.
On baptism the Confession parts from Westminster, confessing immersion of professing believers alone.

etymology: Named for the German imperial city of Augsburg, where it was presented to the Diet in 1530; drafted chiefly by Philipp Melanchthon.
biblical_def: The Augsburg Confession is the foundational symbol of the Lutheran churches, laid before the Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530 and penned largely by Melanchthon under Luther's eye. It is to be honored, for its central articles ring with the gospel. It confesses that men cannot be justified before God by their own strength, merits, or works, but are justified freely for Christ's sake through faith, when they believe that they are received into favor and that their sins are forgiven for His sake. Here is the doctrine that shook Christendom, the article on which the church stands or falls, and we gladly own its truth. Yet on other heads the Confession reveals the differences that would mark the Lutheran way. It teaches that the true body and blood of Christ are truly present and distributed under the form of bread and wine, a sacramental union the Reformed cannot confess, holding rather a spiritual feeding by faith through the Spirit. Its retention of certain rites and its account of the church and ministry likewise differ from the gathered, regulated worship our standards require. We therefore receive the Augsburg Confession as a noble witness to justification by faith while marking, in love and candor, the points at which it stops short of the fuller Reformed confession.
webster_summary: The 1530 Lutheran confession, drafted by Melanchthon, notable for its articles on justification by faith and its account of the sacraments.
webster_full: AUGSBURG CONFESSION, noun [from Augsburg, the German city.] The chief confession of the Lutheran church, presented to the Diet of Augsburg in 1530.
Composed principally by Philipp Melanchthon with Luther's approval.
Confesses justification freely for Christ's sake through faith, apart from human merit.
Teaches the true bodily presence of Christ distributed in the Supper, differing from the Reformed.
“Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.” Romans 3:28.
scriptures: Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Gal 2:16

Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
Rom 4:5
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
Php 3:9
And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:
corruption_summary: A Lutheran confession honored for its gospel; its differences are confessional, not a postmodern distortion.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the purity of justification by faith. The Augsburg Confession states it nobly—men are justified freely for Christ's sake through faith, not by works or merit—and modern evangelicalism, which so often smuggles human decision and performance back into salvation, would do well to relearn it from this very text.

Where the Confession differs from the Reformed lies chiefly in the Supper. Its teaching of Christ's true bodily presence under the bread and wine the Reformed cannot own, confessing instead that believers feed upon the ascended Christ spiritually, by faith and the Spirit. We name the difference plainly, neither flattening it nor letting it eclipse the shared and precious confession that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
roots_summary: The name is geographical, fixed to the city where the confession was read aloud.
roots_lines: Augsburg — the free imperial city in Bavaria.
confession — Latin confiteor, to acknowledge openly.
Presented before the Diet of Augsburg, 25 June 1530.
Authored chiefly by Melanchthon, the mild colleague of Luther.
The first and foundational symbol of the Lutheran churches.
usage: The Augsburg Confession confessed justification by faith before the assembled princes and the Emperor himself.
On the Supper the Augsburg Confession set the Lutheran course that diverged from the Reformed.
We read the Augsburg Confession with thanksgiving for its gospel and with discernment for its differences.

etymology: From Latin formula, a set form, and concordia, agreement; named as the form that restored concord among quarreling Lutherans.
biblical_def: The Formula of Concord is the last of the great Lutheran symbols, drawn up in 1577 and gathered with the older confessions into the Book of Concord of 1580. It was framed to settle the bitter disputes that broke out among Lutherans after Luther's death—quarrels over free will, good works, the third use of the law, original sin, and above all the Lord's Supper. In settling these, the Formula hardened the very points at which Lutheranism stands apart from the Reformed faith. It confessed the oral eating of the true body and blood of Christ by all communicants, worthy and unworthy alike, and to defend this it embraced the doctrine of the ubiquity of Christ's human nature—that His body, by communication of the divine attributes, is present everywhere. The Reformed churches rejected both teachings. We confess that the man Christ Jesus is in heaven according to His humanity until He come again, and that the wicked, receiving the bare elements, do not receive Christ at all, while believers feed on Him spiritually by faith. The Formula also expressly condemned the Reformed understanding of the Supper as a Sacramentarian error. So while we honor the Lutherans' concern to guard against synergism and to uphold grace, the Formula marks the mature parting of the ways, and our standards lead us another road.
webster_summary: The 1577 Lutheran symbol that resolved internal disputes, fixing the doctrines of the bodily presence and the ubiquity of Christ's humanity against the Reformed view.
webster_full: FORMULA OF CONCORD, noun [Latin formula, a form, and concordia, agreement.] The last of the Lutheran confessions, drawn up in 1577 to compose the disputes within Lutheranism.
Gathered with the older symbols into the Book of Concord, 1580.
Teaches the oral eating of Christ's body by all who partake, and the ubiquity of His human nature.
Expressly condemns the Reformed doctrine of the Supper as a Sacramentarian error.
“Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things.” Acts 3:21.
scriptures: Act 3:21
Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began.
Joh 16:7
Nevertheless I tell you the truth; It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you.
So then after the Lord had spoken unto them, he was received up into heaven, and sat on the right hand of God.
Joh 6:63
It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.
corruption_summary: A Lutheran symbol whose departures from the Reformed are confessional, not a modern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the true and abiding humanity of Christ. The Formula's doctrine of ubiquity—that Christ's body is present everywhere—dissolves the reality of His manhood, whereas Scripture says the heaven must receive Him until the restitution of all things. A body that is everywhere is no longer a body; the Reformed confession guards the genuine humanity of our ascended Lord.

The Formula also condemned the Reformed view of the Supper as Sacramentarian and taught that the unworthy orally eat Christ's very flesh. But our Lord Himself taught that the flesh profiteth nothing and the Spirit quickeneth. We confess that the wicked receive only bread to their judgment, while believers feed on the heavenly Christ by faith through the Spirit. The difference is real and we name it, even as we respect the Lutherans' stand against synergism.
roots_summary: The title means the “form of agreement,” from Latin words for a set form and concord.
roots_lines: formula — Latin, a small form or fixed pattern.
concordia — Latin, agreement, harmony of hearts.
Named for the concord it sought among divided Lutherans.
Completed 1577; printed in the Book of Concord, 1580.
Its agreement was Lutheran inward, but a fence outward toward the Reformed.
usage: The Formula of Concord settled the Lutheran disputes by codifying the ubiquity of Christ's body.
Because the Formula condemned the Reformed Supper, the breach between the traditions was sealed.
Our divines answered the Formula of Concord from Acts 3, that heaven must receive Christ until He come.

etymology: Named for the town of Orange (Latin Arausio) in southern Gaul, where the synod met in 529; council from Latin concilium, an assembly.
biblical_def: The Council of Orange, convened in AD 529 under the presidency of Caesarius of Arles, is one of the brightest patristic witnesses to the doctrines of grace and a true forerunner of the Reformed faith. It met to condemn semi-Pelagianism, the cunning compromise that granted man a corrupted will yet left him able to take the first step toward God—to begin to believe—before grace was given. Orange swept this away. It decreed that not only the increase but the very beginning of faith and the longing to believe are the work of the Holy Spirit within us, that grace is not given according to our merits but goes before all our good willing and working. It confessed that by Adam's sin the whole man, body and soul, was changed for the worse, and that no one of himself has anything but lying and sin. Here is the substance of total depravity and the priority of grace, the very marrow our standards would later confess in fuller form. The council affirmed too that God predestines men to good, and it anathematized the dreadful error that any are predestined to evil by divine power—a careful witness the Reformed gladly own, for our doctrine of reprobation is a passing by, not a positive authoring of sin. Orange shows that monergism is no Genevan novelty but the ancient faith.
webster_summary: The synod of AD 529 that condemned semi-Pelagianism and affirmed the priority of grace and predestination unto good, anticipating Reformed soteriology.
webster_full: COUNCIL OF ORANGE, noun [from Orange, Latin Arausio, in Gaul.] A synod held in 529 under Caesarius of Arles to settle the controversy over grace and free will.
Condemned semi-Pelagianism, the teaching that man begins to believe before grace.
Affirmed that the very beginning of faith is the gift of the Holy Spirit.
Confessed the predestination of men unto good and anathematized predestination unto evil.
“For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.” Philippians 2:13.
scriptures: Php 2:13
For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.
Joh 6:44
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
Eph 2:1
And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;
For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?
corruption_summary: An ancient council whose teaching is sound; the danger is a revived semi-Pelagianism that flatters the natural will.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the priority of grace over the will. Orange condemned semi-Pelagianism—the notion that the sinner takes the first step toward God before grace moves him—and the same error lives on wherever men preach that God helps those who help themselves, or that conversion begins with the unaided human decision.

Modern revivalism and free-will religion repeat the very compromise Orange anathematized, making grace a response to man's initiative rather than its cause. But Scripture asks, “what hast thou that thou didst not receive?” and answers that God works in us both to will and to do. To recover Orange is to recover monergism: the dead are quickened, the unwilling are made willing, and from first to last salvation is of the Lord.
roots_summary: The name fixes the council to a Gallic town; council springs from the Latin for an assembly called together.
roots_lines: Orange — from Latin Arausio, a town in southern Gaul.
concilium — Latin, an assembly summoned for counsel.
Convened in 529 under Caesarius, bishop of Arles.
Drew heavily on Augustine against the heirs of Pelagius.
A patristic seedbed of the later Reformed doctrine of grace.
usage: Long before Geneva, the Council of Orange confessed that the beginning of faith is the gift of the Spirit.
We answered the free-will preacher from the Council of Orange, which condemned his semi-Pelagianism by name.
The Council of Orange shows that sovereign grace is the ancient faith, not a sixteenth-century invention.

etymology: The title of J. Gresham Machen's 1923 book; liberalism from Latin liber, free, here naming a theology that frees itself from the supernatural.
biblical_def: Christianity and Liberalism is J. Gresham Machen's 1923 work, written at the height of the modernist controversy in the Northern Presbyterian Church, and it remains one of the sharpest defenses of the faith in the English tongue. Machen's thesis is plain and devastating: theological liberalism is not a variety of Christianity at all, but a different religion springing from a different root, wearing Christian words to mask an alien creed. Liberalism, he showed, denies the supernatural—it cannot abide a God who breaks in from above, a Bible that is His inerrant word, a virgin-born and miracle-working Christ, a substitutionary atonement for sin, or a bodily resurrection. In place of these it offers a religion of human goodness, the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, with Jesus as a teacher and example rather than a Saviour who shed His blood. Machen argued that the two cannot dwell together in one church under one set of vows, for they part on the very nature of God, of man, of sin, and of salvation. The book exposes the deceit of using orthodox language to convey heterodox meaning, and it summons the church to honesty and to faithfulness. We commend it as a trumpet against the modernist apostasy, a defense of the gospel that Machen would shortly suffer to uphold, losing his pulpit but keeping the faith.
webster_summary: Machen's 1923 book arguing that theological liberalism is a distinct religion, not Christianity, because it denies the supernatural gospel.
webster_full: CHRISTIANITY AND LIBERALISM, noun [from liber, Latin, free.] The 1923 book by J. Gresham Machen contending that liberalism and Christianity are two separate religions.
Written amid the fundamentalist-modernist controversy in the Presbyterian Church.
Shows liberalism to deny the inerrant Scripture, the deity and miracles of Christ, and His atoning death.
Exposes the use of orthodox words to convey an unbelieving meaning.
“Though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you... let him be accursed.” Galatians 1:8.
scriptures: Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;
Jud 1:4

For there are certain men crept in unawares, who were before of old ordained to this condemnation, ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness, and denying the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ.

For if he that cometh preacheth another Jesus, whom we have not preached, or if ye receive another spirit, which ye have not received, or another gospel, which ye have not accepted, ye might well bear with him.
corruption_summary: Liberalism is itself the corruption Machen named: a counterfeit religion that empties the gospel of the supernatural while keeping its vocabulary.
corruption_paragraphs: Theological liberalism, the very target of Machen's book, is the great corruption of the modern church. It denies that the Bible is the inerrant word of God, recasts the virgin birth and resurrection as myth, and reduces the atoning death of Christ to a moral example. In their place it preaches a religion of human progress and the inherent goodness of man. By Galatians' verdict, this is “another gospel,” and the apostle pronounces it accursed.

Its peculiar deceit is the retention of Christian words—sin, salvation, faith, even God and Christ—poured full of unbelieving meaning, so that the unwary hear orthodoxy where heresy is meant. Machen's answer, and ours, is that liberalism is not a wing of the church but a rival religion that has “crept in unawares.” Honesty demands we say so, and faithfulness demands we contend for the supernatural gospel once delivered to the saints, the only gospel that saves.
roots_summary: The key word liberalism springs from Latin liber, free—a theology that frees itself from revealed authority.
roots_lines: liber — Latin, free, the root of liberty and liberalism.
-ism — suffix marking a system or doctrine.
In theology, the freeing of religion from the supernatural and the inerrant word.
Christianity, by contrast, binds itself to God's revelation.
Machen set the two side by side and showed them to be two religions.
usage: Machen's Christianity and Liberalism still arms the church against the modernist who keeps the words but denies the faith.
He read Christianity and Liberalism and saw at last that the liberal preacher served another gospel altogether.
By the thesis of Christianity and Liberalism, a denial of the bodily resurrection is not weak Christianity but no Christianity.

etymology: From Latin fundamentum, a foundation; the title of a series of essays defending the foundational doctrines of the faith.
biblical_def: The Fundamentals were a series of ninety essays published in twelve volumes between 1910 and 1915, funded by two Christian laymen and edited in part by R. A. Torrey, sent freely to ministers, missionaries, and students across the English-speaking world. They were raised up to answer the rising tide of modernism, which under the banner of higher criticism and evolutionary thought was hollowing out the seminaries and pulpits. Against this assault the essays defended the great foundations: the inspiration and inerrancy of the Holy Scriptures, the deity of our Lord Jesus Christ, His virgin birth, His substitutionary atonement for sinners, and His bodily resurrection from the dead. They answered the documentary dismemberment of Moses' books, defended the historicity of the miracles, and held up the gospel of grace against a religion of mere morality. From this great labor the name “fundamentalist” was later taken, denoting one who holds fast these non-negotiable doctrines. Though the essays came from a broad coalition and were not uniformly Reformed in their detail—some leaning dispensational, some Arminian—their witness to the supernatural gospel was clear and courageous. We honor The Fundamentals as a worthy stand for the faith once delivered, a line drawn in a perilous hour, and we receive their core convictions as nothing less than the truth that must be believed and confessed in every age.
webster_summary: A 1910–1915 essay series defending the inerrancy of Scripture and the core supernatural doctrines of the faith against modernism.
webster_full: THE FUNDAMENTALS, noun [Latin fundamentum, a foundation.] A series of ninety essays in twelve volumes, published 1910 to 1915 in defense of the essential Christian doctrines.
Edited in part by R. A. Torrey and distributed freely to ministers worldwide.
Defended the inspiration and inerrancy of Scripture against higher criticism.
Upheld the deity, virgin birth, atoning death, and bodily resurrection of Christ.
“Other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.” 1 Corinthians 3:11.

corruption_summary: An essay series defending the faith; the corruption it opposed is the very modernism that still denies inerrancy and the supernatural Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the very burden of these essays: the foundational, non-negotiable doctrines of the faith. Modernism, which The Fundamentals arose to answer, dismembered the Scriptures by higher criticism, denied the virgin birth, and recast the atonement and resurrection as symbol—and that unbelief is far from dead in the seminaries and pulpits of our day.

A second danger is the corruption of the word “fundamentalist” itself, which the world now wields as a slur for any narrow or violent zealot. But Scripture says no other foundation can be laid than Jesus Christ, and to hold the fundamentals is simply to hold the gospel. To recover The Fundamentals is to recover both the doctrines they defended and the courage to confess them when the academy mocks.

etymology: From English great and ejection, Latin ejicere, to cast out; the casting out of Puritan ministers under the Act of Uniformity of 1662.
biblical_def: The Great Ejection was the casting out of some two thousand Puritan ministers from the Church of England in 1662, when the Act of Uniformity required every clergyman to give his unfeigned assent and consent to all that was contained in the restored Book of Common Prayer. Upon St. Bartholomew's Day, the twenty-fourth of August, those who could not in conscience subscribe were stripped of their livings, their pulpits, and their bread. Rather than violate the dictates of conscience and the regulative principle of worship, men such as Richard Baxter, Thomas Watson, Joseph Alleine, and Edmund Calamy laid down all and went out, many to poverty, imprisonment, and harassment under the Conventicle and Five Mile Acts that followed. This day gave birth to English Nonconformity and Dissent—the Presbyterians, Congregationalists, and Baptists who would worship God according to His word rather than the prescriptions of men. We honor these ejected ministers as faithful confessors who counted Christ's lordship over conscience dearer than place and comfort. Out of their suffering came a golden harvest of Puritan devotional and theological writing, penned by men who had leisure forced upon them and turned it to the church's lasting good. Their example rebukes every easy compromise and teaches that the worship of God is not ours to amend at the magistrate's command, but His to prescribe and ours to obey.
webster_summary: The 1662 expulsion of around two thousand Puritan ministers from the Church of England under the Act of Uniformity, the founding event of English Nonconformity.
webster_full: GREAT EJECTION, noun [Latin ejicere, to cast out.] The expulsion of about two thousand Puritan ministers from their livings in 1662 for refusing the Act of Uniformity.
Took effect on St. Bartholomew's Day, 24 August 1662.
Required assent to the restored Book of Common Prayer, which these men could not in conscience give.
Gave rise to English Nonconformity—Presbyterian, Congregational, and Baptist Dissent.

corruption_summary: A historic act of faithful suffering; the danger is forgetting it and yielding conscience to the convenience of conformity.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the supremacy of conscience bound to God's word over the commands of men in worship. The ejected ministers would not subscribe to a liturgy they judged unwarranted by Scripture, and they paid with their livings. Peter's rule governed them: we ought to obey God rather than men.

Our soft age, which prizes ease and acceptance, struggles to grasp such costly fidelity, and there is a steady temptation to amend the worship of God to the taste of men or the demand of the state. To recover the Great Ejection is to recover the regulative principle—that God alone prescribes how He shall be worshipped—and the courage to suffer loss rather than bind the conscience or bow to an unscriptural conformity.

etymology: From covenant, Latin convenire, to come together in agreement, with the agent suffix -er; one who swore the Scottish national covenants.
biblical_def: A Covenanter was a Scottish Presbyterian who swore and upheld the great national covenants—the National Covenant of 1638 and the Solemn League and Covenant of 1643—binding the nation to maintain the Reformed religion and to resist the imposition of prelacy and the king's claim to headship over the church. They confessed that Christ alone is King and Head of His church, and that no earthly monarch may usurp His crown rights or prescribe how He shall be worshipped. When the Stuart kings broke faith and forced episcopacy and a royal supremacy upon Scotland, the Covenanters would not yield. Driven from their pulpits, they gathered in the open fields for conventicle worship, preaching and praying upon the moors with sentinels posted against the dragoons. There followed the bitter years remembered as the “Killing Time,” the 1680s, when men, women, and even the young were shot, drowned, or hanged for their refusal to forswear the covenants or to own the king as head of the church. Such were the martyrs of the Wigtown sands and the Grassmarket scaffold. We honor the Covenanters as witnesses to the crown rights of the Redeemer and to the regulative principle of worship, men and women who esteemed the lordship of Christ over conscience worth their very blood, and whose steadfastness watered the Reformed church in Scotland and beyond.
webster_summary: A Scottish Presbyterian who upheld the National Covenant and Solemn League and Covenant, asserting Christ's sole headship over the church even unto martyrdom.
webster_full: COVENANTER, noun [from covenant, Latin convenire, to agree.] One who subscribed and maintained the Scottish national covenants of 1638 and 1643.

corruption_summary: A faithful Scottish witness; the danger is forgetting their stand for Christ's sole kingship over His church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the crown rights of the Redeemer—that Christ alone is King and Head of His church, and no earthly power may usurp His throne or dictate His worship. The Covenanters died confessing it; the modern church too easily forgets it, ceding to the state or the spirit of the age what belongs to Christ alone.

There is also a temptation to romanticize their suffering while shrinking from their conviction. But the Covenanters were no mere patriots; they were confessors who held the lordship of Christ over conscience dearer than life, faithful unto death for the crown of life. To recover their witness is to honor the regulative principle of worship and to confess, with Psalm 2, that God has set His King upon His holy hill of Zion.
